tool.name: Terraform
tool.tagline: Define cloud infrastructure as code and apply changes with a reviewable plan
tool.description: Terraform describes infrastructure (networks, servers, databases, DNS, SaaS settings) in HCL files, shows a plan of what will change, and applies it through providers for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes and thousands of other APIs. It is the most widely used infrastructure-as-code tool; OpenTofu is its open-source fork with the same language.

glossary.def: HashiCorp Configuration Language: the simple language Terraform files (.tf) are written in, made of named blocks holding name = value settings.
A Terraform add-on program that knows one service, such as AWS or GitHub, and turns Terraform's requests into that service's API calls.
One thing in your infrastructure, such as a virtual machine, a storage bucket or a DNS record. In Terraform, each is declared with a resource block.
The basic computing pieces an app runs on: servers, storage, networks, databases and the settings that connect them.
Terraform's record of the real things it manages: which real object each resource in your files stands for, and its last known details.
A named place for files in cloud storage, like an online folder; Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage keep files in buckets.
The public online catalogue at registry.terraform.io where providers and shared modules are published, with documentation for every resource type.
A Terraform data block that only reads information about something that already exists, such as an account ID or a machine image, without managing it.
Amazon Machine Image: a ready-made starting copy of a machine's software, such as Ubuntu Linux, from which new AWS virtual machines are started.
The place where Terraform keeps its state: a local file by default, or shared storage such as a cloud bucket, usually with locking so two runs can't change it at once.
A setting Terraform itself understands on any resource or module block, such as count, for_each, depends_on or lifecycle, rather than one defined by a provider.
A folder of Terraform files. The one you run commands in is the root module; it can call other folders as child modules, passing values in and reading their outputs.
In Terraform, one of several named states kept for the same set of files, chosen with terraform workspace select. HCP Terraform uses the word for a richer idea.
A Terraform construct that generates repeated nested blocks inside a resource from a list or map, instead of writing each block out.
A Terraform block recording that a resource's address changed, so Terraform renames it in state instead of destroying and recreating it.
A Terraform block that adopts an existing real object, such as a bucket made by hand, so Terraform manages it from then on.
A Terraform block that stops managing a resource, optionally without deleting the real object.
Differences between Terraform's state and the real infrastructure, caused by changes made outside Terraform, such as edits in the web console.
HashiCorp's online service that stores Terraform state and runs plans and applies for teams, with approvals and permissions.
A free, community-run fork of Terraform with the same language and commands, started in 2023 after Terraform's licence changed.
A widely used way for one program to call functions in another over a connection, sending small, compact messages.
A Terraform block that fetches something short-lived, such as a secret or a temporary password, for the length of one run without saving it in state.
A resource setting, such as password_wo, that Terraform sends to the provider but never saves in state or plan files.

concepts.name: Cloud infrastructure in plain words
concepts.summary: The servers, storage and networks Terraform builds, and the cloud companies that rent them out, explained from scratch.
concepts.why: Terraform's whole job is creating these things, so you need a clear picture of them before writing a single line.
takeaways: A cloud provider rents out servers, storage, databases and networks by the hour
The things you rent are resources; together they are your infrastructure
Programs create resources through the cloud provider's API, using secret credentials
pitfalls: Sharing or committing cloud credentials: anyone holding them can use your account and run up charges.

quiz.q: What is a cloud provider's API for?
options: Letting programs ask the provider to create, change or delete resources
quiz.explain: The API is the menu of requests programs can send; Terraform uses it to manage your resources.

quiz.q: What is a storage bucket used for?
options: Turning a name like shop.example.com into an address
Holding files, such as uploaded photos
quiz.explain: A bucket is an online folder for files; the other answers describe virtual machines, DNS and permissions.

concepts.name: Infrastructure as code and Terraform
concepts.summary: Describe your infrastructure in files kept in Git, and let Terraform work out and make the changes.
concepts.why: Clicking in a web console can't be reviewed or repeated; files can.
concepts.body:
Picture setting up a website by clicking through a cloud provider's web console: a virtual machine here, a bucket there, a DNS record. It works, but a month later nobody remembers exactly what was clicked, a second copy for testing comes out slightly different, and nobody reviewed any of it.

**Infrastructure as code** (IaC) means writing your infrastructure down in text files instead, kept in Git like any project. Changes are reviewed before they happen, a copy can be rebuilt from the same files, and the files document what exists.

Terraform is **declarative**: you describe the end result you want ("a bucket named photos that keeps old versions of files"), not the clicks to get there, and Terraform works out the steps. You write in **HCL**, Terraform's own simple language, in files ending in `.tf`.

The everyday cycle has two commands:

- `terraform plan` compares your files with what exists and lists what it would create, change or destroy. Nothing is touched yet.
- `terraform apply` carries out those changes.

To know what exists, Terraform keeps its **state**: its own record of every resource it created, such as which real bucket belongs to which part of your files.

Terraform itself knows no cloud. For each service it downloads a **provider**: an add-on program that turns Terraform's instructions into that service's API calls. There are providers for AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, GitHub, Cloudflare and thousands of other services.

Alternatives exist: CloudFormation and Bicep work with one cloud only, Pulumi lets you write general programming code, and Ansible sets up software on existing machines rather than creating them (the two are often used together). **OpenTofu** is a free community fork of Terraform, made after Terraform's licence changed in 2023; for everything in this course it behaves the same, with `tofu` in place of `terraform`.

The big rule: once Terraform manages something, change it only through Terraform, not the console, or the next plan will try to undo your manual change.
takeaways: Describe the end result; Terraform works out and makes the changes
plan shows the changes before apply makes them
Providers talk to each service; state records what Terraform manages
pitfalls: Changing Terraform-managed resources in the console, then being surprised when apply undoes the change.

quiz.q: What does terraform plan do?
options: Shows the changes needed to make reality match the configuration
quiz.explain: plan is a dry run: it works out and shows the changes without making any.

concepts.name: Providers and terraform init
concepts.summary: Say which providers you need and which versions are allowed, then prepare the project folder with terraform init.
concepts.why: Every project starts with init, and providers left free to update are a classic source of surprise breakage.
concepts.body:
Each provider is a separate program, published in the **Terraform Registry**, the online catalogue of providers at `registry.terraform.io`. You list the ones you need in a `terraform` block (a named section of a `.tf` file, wrapped in curly braces):

- `source` says where to download it, like `hashicorp/aws`: the publisher, then the provider's name.
- `version` says which versions are allowed. Providers release often, and a new major version (the first number, as in 6 to 7) may change how things work. `~> 6.0` means at least 6.0 but below 7.0; `~> 6.2.1` means at least 6.2.1 but below 6.3.0; `>= 1.2, < 2.0` spells it out.
- `required_version` limits which versions of Terraform itself may run the files.

`terraform init` prepares the folder. It downloads the providers into a hidden `.terraform/` folder and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`, a **lock file** recording the exact provider versions it picked, plus a **checksum** of each: a fingerprint of the download, so a corrupted or tampered copy is spotted.

Commit the lock file to Git, so teammates and automated runs use exactly the same providers. To move to newer versions on purpose, within your limits, run `terraform init -upgrade`. Rerun `init` whenever you add a provider; `plan` reminds you if you forget. Init also prepares a few other things you'll meet later.

A `provider` block configures one provider: its region, default labels (`tags`) stuck on every resource it creates, and how it signs in. Keep credentials out of your files: let the provider find them on your computer, for example through the `AWS_PROFILE` setting that names a saved AWS login.

To use one provider in two ways, say in two regions, give the second block an `alias` and point a resource at it with `provider = aws.us`.
takeaways: required_providers lists providers and allowed versions; ~> lets only the last number grow
init downloads providers and writes .terraform.lock.hcl: commit it
Use alias for a second configuration of the same provider
pitfalls: Not committing .terraform.lock.hcl, so automated runs quietly pick a newer provider than you tested.

quiz.q: Which provider versions does the constraint ~> 6.0 allow?
quiz.explain: With two numbers, ~> lets the second number grow but not the first.

concepts.name: Resources, arguments and references
concepts.summary: Write resource blocks, set their arguments, and connect resources by referring to each other's attributes.
concepts.why: Resources are the heart of every configuration, and pointing one at another tells Terraform what to create first.
concepts.body:
A `resource` block declares one thing you want to exist:

`resource "<TYPE>" "<NAME>" { ...settings... }`

The type, such as `aws_instance` (an AWS virtual machine) or `google_storage_bucket`, comes from a provider. The name is your own label. Together they form the resource's **address**, like `aws_instance.web`, which must be unique.

Inside the braces, **arguments** set what the resource should look like, one `name = value` per line. Values can be text in double quotes (a **string**), numbers, `true` or `false`, lists in square brackets like `["a", "b"]`, and maps in braces like `{ team = "web" }`, which pair names with values. Some settings are blocks of their own, nested inside.

Once created, a resource also has **attributes**: facts you can read about it, including ones the cloud decides, such as the ID it assigned. Every resource type's arguments and attributes are listed on its page in the Terraform Registry; that page will be your main guide.

To use one resource's attribute in another, write `<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>`, like `aws_vpc.main.id`. Here `aws_vpc` is a **VPC**, your own private network in the cloud, and a subnet is a smaller section of it. Such a **reference** also tells Terraform about a dependency: it creates the network before the subnet that needs its ID, and destroys them in the opposite order.

Some attributes aren't known until the resource exists, such as a new ID. Plans show them as `(known after apply)`.

A few writing rules: `#` starts a comment, `${...}` inside a string inserts a value (`"app-${var.env}"`), and `<<-EOT` ... `EOT` holds text spanning several lines. All `.tf` files in one folder count as one configuration, so splitting them into `main.tf`, `network.tf` and so on is just for tidiness.

`terraform fmt` lays your files out in the standard style, and `terraform validate` checks them for mistakes; run both before every commit.
concepts.code:
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {                  # a private network
  cidr_block           = "10.0.0.0/16"        # its range of internal addresses
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags                 = { Name = "main" }    # labels shown in the AWS console
}

resource "aws_subnet" "app" {                 # a smaller section of that network
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id         # reference: create the VPC first
  cidr_block        = "10.0.1.0/24"
  availability_zone = "eu-west-1a"            # one data centre in the region
  tags              = { Name = "app-${aws_vpc.main.tags.Name}" }
}
# terraform plan
#   + resource "aws_subnet" "app" {
#       + id     = (known after apply)
#       + vpc_id = (known after apply)
takeaways: resource "type" "name" gives the address type.name
Referring to aws_vpc.main.id makes Terraform create the VPC first
All .tf files in a folder are one configuration; run `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate`
pitfalls: Renaming a resource and being surprised the plan destroys and recreates it (a `moved` block, covered later, prevents that).

quiz.q: Why does Terraform create aws_vpc.main before aws_subnet.app here?
quiz.explain: The reference makes the subnet depend on the VPC, so Terraform creates the VPC first.

concepts.name: plan, apply and destroy
concepts.summary: Read the symbols in a plan, apply exactly what was reviewed, and destroy what you no longer need.
concepts.why: Reading a plan correctly is the single most important safety skill in Terraform.
concepts.body:
`terraform plan` prints each change with a symbol:

- `+` create, `-` destroy, `~` change in place (the resource stays; one of its settings changes).
- `-/+` **replace**: destroy, then create a new one (or `+/-`, creating first). Some settings can't be changed on an existing resource, and the plan marks the one responsible with `# forces replacement`.

The summary line `Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.` deserves a pause whenever destroy isn't zero. Replacing a database or a **disk** (a virtual machine's storage drive) can mean losing its data, and replacing a DNS zone can take a website offline.

`terraform apply` plans again, shows the plan and asks you to type `yes`. When a program runs Terraform for you, save the plan and apply exactly that:

- `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, then `terraform apply tfplan`. A saved plan is applied only if nothing has changed since; it never does something different from what was reviewed.
- `terraform show tfplan` prints a saved plan again.

Other options:

- `-var` and `-var-file` give values to variables (next lesson).
- `-target=aws_instance.web` limits the run to one resource and what it depends on: an emergency escape hatch, not a habit.
- `-replace=aws_instance.web` forces one resource to be rebuilt.
- `terraform destroy` removes everything the configuration manages; `terraform plan -destroy` previews that.

Plans can't foresee everything. Some errors appear only when the provider actually calls the API, such as a name that is already taken or an account **quota** (a limit on how many of something you may have) that is used up. Apply then stops part-way. Fix the problem and apply again; Terraform carries on from what its state recorded.
concepts.code:
terraform plan -out=tfplan
#   # aws_db_instance.main must be replaced
# -/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
#       ~ engine_version = "16.4" -> "17.2" # forces replacement (a new database!)
# Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt   # save it to attach to the review
terraform apply tfplan
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web    # rebuild one virtual machine
terraform plan -destroy                      # preview tearing everything down
takeaways: + create, ~ update, - destroy, -/+ replace
Pause on any destroy or forces replacement
plan -out then apply the saved plan in automation
pitfalls: Applying without reading the plan, and replacing a live database because one changed argument forced replacement.

quiz.q: A plan line shows -/+ next to a resource. What will happen?
options: The resource will be destroyed and recreated
quiz.explain: -/+ means replacement, usually because an argument can't be changed in place.

concepts.name: Input variables and outputs
concepts.summary: Make configurations adjustable with typed input variables, set them from files or when running a command, and show results with outputs.
concepts.why: Variables make one configuration reusable across environments; outputs pass values to people and other code.
concepts.body:
An input **variable** is a setting your configuration accepts from outside, like a blank on a form: the environment's name, a machine size. Declare it with a `variable` block and use it as `var.name`. Inside the block:

- `type`: what kind of value it takes. `string` (text), `number`, `bool` (`true` or `false`), `list(string)` (several strings in order), `map(number)` (names paired with numbers), or `object({ name = string, size = optional(number, 10) })` for a group of named parts of different kinds.
- `default`: a value used when none is given, which makes the variable optional.
- `description`: explains the variable to whoever fills it in.
- `sensitive = true`: hides the value in plan output.
- `nullable = false`: refuses **null**, Terraform's special value meaning "nothing".

Values can come from several places. From weakest to strongest: the default; an **environment variable** named `TF_VAR_name` (a named setting held by your open terminal window, which programs started from it can read); a `terraform.tfvars` file; `*.auto.tfvars` files; then `-var-file=...` and `-var name=value` typed with the command. The strongest one wins.

If a variable without a default gets no value, Terraform stops and asks you to type one. That's fine at your desk, but an automated run would wait forever.

A common pattern is one `.tfvars` file per environment: `terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars`.

An **output** shows a value after apply: `output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id }`. Outputs are printed at the end of apply and can be read any time with `terraform output` (`-raw name` prints just one value, handy for other programs; `-json` prints all). Later you'll see outputs also pass values between parts of a larger setup.

Mark outputs that contain secrets `sensitive = true`. They are then hidden on screen, but still saved, readable, in the state.
takeaways: Typed variables with defaults, descriptions and optional() parts
Strength: default < TF_VAR_ < tfvars < auto.tfvars < -var-file/-var
Outputs show results; sensitive hides them on screen, not in state
pitfalls: Leaving variables without values in automated runs, so Terraform waits for someone to type them.

quiz.q: environment is set to dev in terraform.tfvars and to prod with -var on the command line. Which wins?
options: Whichever was set last in the file
quiz.explain: Values given with -var and -var-file on the command are the strongest.

concepts.name: What state is and why it matters
concepts.summary: Terraform's state maps your configuration to real resource IDs; protect it, never commit it, and never edit it by hand.
concepts.why: Losing or corrupting state is the worst common Terraform accident.
concepts.body:
Terraform's **state** is a file (`terraform.tfstate` by default) written in **JSON**, a common text format for structured data. For each resource address it records the real thing it stands for: its ID and everything Terraform knows about it. Terraform needs it because:

- A cloud API can't tell which real things belong to which blocks in your files; `aws_instance.web` is linked to the real machine `i-0abc...` only through state.
- It keeps attribute values that other resources depend on, and makes plans faster.
- It remembers resources you deleted from your files, so Terraform can destroy them.

During plan, Terraform first **refreshes**: it asks the API for each resource's current settings, then compares your files against them.

Rules:

- **Never commit state to Git.** It holds secrets in readable form, such as database passwords and secret keys, and two people with different copies will overwrite each other's work. Add `*.tfstate`, `*.tfstate.*` and the `.terraform/` folder to `.gitignore`, but do commit `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
- For any project you share, keep state in a **remote backend**: shared storage, such as a cloud bucket, with locking so two people can't change it at once (next level).
- Don't edit it by hand. Look with `terraform state list` and `terraform state show`, and change it with Terraform's own tools (covered later).
- Losing state doesn't delete anything in the cloud, but Terraform forgets those resources exist, and the next apply tries to create them again. Recovering means adopting each one again by hand.
concepts.code:
terraform state list
# aws_subnet.app
# aws_vpc.main
terraform state show aws_vpc.main | head -5    # first 5 lines of what state knows
# resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
#     arn        = "arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:123456789012:vpc/vpc-0a1b2c3d"
#     cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
#     id         = "vpc-0a1b2c3d"

# add these lines to .gitignore
cat >> .gitignore <<'EOF'
.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
*.tfplan
EOF
takeaways: State links addresses like aws_vpc.main to real IDs
It holds secrets: never commit it; keep it remote with locking
Change state with Terraform's commands, not by hand
pitfalls: Committing terraform.tfstate to a repository, leaking secrets and causing conflicting copies.

quiz.q: You delete terraform.tfstate locally (no remote backend) and run apply. What happens?
options: Terraform rebuilds state from the cloud automatically
Terraform plans to create everything again, likely colliding with existing resources
quiz.explain: Without state Terraform doesn't know the objects exist; it would try to create them anew.

concepts.name: Data sources
concepts.summary: Read details of things that already exist with data blocks, instead of copying their IDs into your files.
concepts.why: Real configurations must refer to things they don't manage: machine images, your account, networks or domains owned by other teams.
concepts.body:
A **data source** reads information without managing anything:

`data "<TYPE>" "<NAME>" { ...filters... }`, and you use its results as `data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>`.

Typical uses:

- Look up the latest machine image: `data "aws_ami"`. An image (an **AMI** in AWS) is a ready-made starting copy of a machine's software, such as Ubuntu Linux, that new virtual machines start from.
- Read the current account and region: `data "aws_caller_identity"`, `data "aws_region"`.
- Find a shared resource owned by another team, such as a network by its label or a domain's DNS records by name.

Data sources can also build documents. AWS writes permissions as **IAM** policies: documents saying who may do what, written in **JSON**, a text format for structured data. `data "aws_iam_policy_document"` produces that text from HCL blocks and checks it, so you don't hand-write it.

`data "terraform_remote_state"` reads the outputs of another Terraform configuration. It's convenient, but it ties you to that configuration's whole state; publishing just the values you need in a shared place is often cleaner.

Data sources are read during planning when their arguments are known. If an argument depends on something not yet created, the read waits until apply, and values from it show as `(known after apply)`.

A data source that finds nothing, or several matches where one is expected, makes the plan fail, which is a useful guard. Be careful with "latest" lookups like `most_recent = true`: when a new image is released, the plan changes and may replace your machines. Pin an exact image, or tell Terraform to ignore that change (covered later), when it matters.
takeaways: data blocks read; resource blocks manage
Use results as data.type.name.attribute
"Latest" lookups change over time and can trigger replacements
pitfalls: Using most_recent image lookups for long-lived machines and getting surprise replacements.

quiz.q: What does Terraform do with an object found by a data source when you run destroy?
quiz.explain: Data sources only read information; Terraform never manages their objects.

concepts.name: Expressions, types and conditionals
concepts.summary: Compute values in HCL with types, operators, if-else choices and for expressions.
concepts.why: Almost every real configuration reshapes lists and maps; expressions are how.
concepts.body:
An **expression** is any piece of HCL that produces a value: `"web"`, `3`, `var.env`, or a calculation like `var.size * 2`. Every value has a type: `string`, `number`, `bool`, the collections `list(...)`, `set(...)` (no order, no duplicates) and `map(...)`, plus `object({...})` and `tuple([...])` for mixed groups. Terraform converts between types where it's safe (`"5"` to `5`) and stops with an error where it isn't.

Expressions you'll use constantly:

- Inserting values into text: `"web-${var.env}"`.
- Choosing between two values with a **conditional**: `var.env == "prod" ? 3 : 1` means: 3 if `env` is `"prod"`, otherwise 1. Both choices must have compatible types.
- **Operators**, the symbols for comparing and combining values: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `&&` (and), `||` (or), `!` (not), arithmetic, and `<`, `>`.

Picking and collecting items:

- `var.subnets[0]` is the first item of a list (counting starts at 0), `var.tags["team"]` the value stored under a name in a map, and `var.cfg.size` one part of an **object** (a group of named values of different kinds).
- A splat, `aws_instance.web[*].id`, collects one attribute from every copy of a resource (copies come later, with `count`).

Building new collections:

- A for expression does something to each item: `[for s in var.names : upper(s)]` builds a list, using the built-in **function** `upper()`, which capitalises text. `{for k, v in var.sizes : k => v * 2}` builds a map. Add `if` to filter: `[for u in var.users : u.name if u.admin]`.
- `null` means "not set", so an argument set to `null` behaves as if you left it out, handy inside conditionals.

Try expressions out with `terraform console`: type one, press Enter, and see its value. It's the fastest way to understand a tricky for expression.
takeaways: A conditional cond ? a : b picks a value; both sides need compatible types
for expressions build lists [...] and maps {...}, with an optional if
Splat [*] collects one attribute from every copy; try things in terraform console
pitfalls: Mixing types in a conditional (a list on one side, a string on the other), which fails.

quiz.q: What is [for n in [1, 2, 3, 4] : n * 10 if n % 2 == 0]?
quiz.explain: The filter keeps 2 and 4, which are then multiplied by 10.

concepts.name: Remote backends and locking
concepts.summary: Store state remotely in S3, GCS, Azure Storage or HCP Terraform, with locking so two runs never collide.
concepts.why: Teams and automated runs must share one true copy of state, and two applies at the same time can corrupt it.
concepts.body:
A **state backend** (usually just called a *backend*) decides where state lives. The default `local` backend writes a file next to your code, fine for experiments only. For anything shared, use a remote backend:

- `s3` (AWS): state in a bucket; locking by writing a small lock object into the bucket, via `use_lockfile = true` (the older locking through a DynamoDB table is being phased out).
- `gcs` (Google Cloud) and `azurerm` (Azure Storage): built-in locking.
- `remote`/`cloud` block for **HCP Terraform** or Terraform Enterprise, which also run plans for you.
- Others: `pg`, `consul`, `kubernetes`, `http`.

**Locking**: an operation that may write state takes a lock first. If someone else holds it, you get "Error acquiring the state lock" with the holder's details. Wait; only use `terraform force-unlock <ID>` when you are sure the holder crashed.

Good practice for the storage itself: enable bucket **versioning** (the bucket keeps every old copy, so you can recover from a bad write), encryption, tight access control and block public access. Create the state bucket once, outside the configuration that uses it (a small bootstrap configuration or by hand).

Backend blocks can't use variables, because init reads them before variables exist. Pass environment-specific settings separately: `terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend`.

Changing backends: update the block and run `terraform init -migrate-state`, which copies the state across.
concepts.code:
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-terraform-state"
    key          = "network/prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true      # S3-native locking (Terraform 1.10+)
  }
}
# terraform init -migrate-state      # move existing local state into S3
# A second concurrent apply:
# Error: Error acquiring the state lock
#   Lock Info:
#     ID:        6f1c9a7e-...
#     Who:       ci@runner-42
#     Operation: OperationTypeApply
takeaways: Use a remote backend with locking for any state more than one person uses
S3 locks with use_lockfile; GCS and Azure lock on their own
Version and encrypt the state bucket; force-unlock only when sure
pitfalls: Using force-unlock while another apply is genuinely still running.

quiz.q: Why can't you write bucket = var.state_bucket in a backend block?
options: Variables are evaluated after the backend is initialised
Buckets must be literal for security
quiz.explain: The backend is configured during init, before variables are processed; use -backend-config instead.

concepts.name: Locals and built-in functions
concepts.summary: Name intermediate values with locals and transform data with built-in functions like merge, lookup and cidrsubnet.
concepts.why: Locals keep configurations readable; functions avoid hard-coding derived values.
concepts.body:
A **local value** names an expression so you can reuse it: define in a `locals` block, use as `local.name`. Use locals for things like a naming prefix, a merged map of labels, or a computed list, so the logic lives in one place. Unlike variables, locals can't be set from outside.

Terraform has a fixed set of built-in **functions** (you can't define your own in HCL, though providers can ship provider-defined functions called as `provider::name::fn(...)`). The ones you'll use most:

- strings: `format`, `join`, `split`, `replace`, `lower`, `trimspace`, `startswith`
- collections: `merge`, `concat`, `flatten`, `lookup(map, key, default)`, `keys`, `values`, `contains`, `distinct`, `zipmap`, `setproduct`
- numbers: `max`, `min`, `ceil`
- converting formats: `jsonencode`, `yamldecode`, `base64encode`
- files: `file` reads a file; `templatefile(path, vars)` fills the placeholders in a text file with values, for settings files and start-up scripts
- networking: `cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum)` and `cidrhost`
- type and errors: `try(expr, fallback)`, `can(expr)`, `coalesce`, `tostring`, `tomap`

`jsonencode` is the right way to produce JSON, for example for permission policies: you can't get the quotes and commas wrong.

Test functions in `terraform console`: `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)` returns `"10.0.2.0/24"`.
takeaways: locals name derived values; variables are inputs
merge, lookup, cidrsubnet, jsonencode, templatefile, try cover most needs
No user-defined HCL functions; try them out in terraform console
pitfalls: Building JSON by gluing values into text instead of using jsonencode, and breaking it on a quote.

quiz.q: What does cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 3) return?
quiz.explain: Adding 8 bits to /16 gives /24 subnets, and netnum 3 selects the fourth one.

concepts.name: count and for_each
concepts.summary: Create several copies of a resource from a number with count, or from a map or set with for_each.
concepts.why: Repetition is everywhere, and choosing count where for_each belongs causes destructive plans later.
concepts.body:
Two **meta-arguments** (settings Terraform itself understands on any resource) make several copies, called instances, from one block:

- **count**: `count = 3` makes `aws_instance.web[0]`, `[1]`, `[2]`, with `count.index` inside. Also the standard way to make a resource **conditional**: `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`.
- **for_each**: takes a **map** or a **set of strings** and makes one instance per key: `aws_iam_user.u["ana"]`, with `each.key` and `each.value` inside.

Why it matters: instances are tracked by position number (count) or by key (for_each). With `count` over a list `["a", "b", "c"]`, removing `"a"` shifts `"b"` to index 0 and `"c"` to 1, so Terraform plans to **change or replace** b and c and destroy the last one. With `for_each`, removing `"a"` destroys only `"a"`. Rule of thumb: use `count` for N identical things or on/off switches; use `for_each` whenever items have identities.

for_each keys must be known at plan time: you can't key on an attribute generated during apply, such as an ID. Use names from your input. Convert a list with `toset(var.names)`, or a list of objects with `{ for o in var.items : o.name => o }`.

Refer to all instances with splat (`aws_instance.web[*].id`, count only) or a for expression (`[for u in aws_iam_user.u : u.arn]`, works for both). Both meta-arguments also work on `module` blocks.
takeaways: count: N copies or on/off; for_each: one instance per key
Removing a list item under count shifts indexes and churns resources
for_each keys must be known at plan time
pitfalls: Using count over a list of names, then deleting the first name and watching every later instance be replaced.

quiz.q: A count-based list of 3 users loses its first element. What does the plan typically show?
options: Changes to the remaining users plus destroying index 2
quiz.explain: Indexes shift: [0] and [1] get new values and [2] is destroyed.

concepts.name: depends_on and the lifecycle block
concepts.summary: Add hidden dependencies with depends_on and control replacement and deletion with lifecycle settings.
concepts.why: Zero-downtime replacements and protection of critical resources come from lifecycle rules.
concepts.body:
Terraform orders operations from references. When a dependency is real but not visible through a reference (an app needs an IAM permission policy, AWS's who-may-do-what rules, attached before it starts, but never uses any of the policy's attributes), add `depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.app]`. Use it sparingly: it makes plans more conservative, because more values become unknown.

The **lifecycle** block changes how changes are carried out:

- `create_before_destroy = true`: when replacement is needed, create the new one first, then destroy the old one. Essential for things in use, such as a website's security certificate or an AWS launch template (the recipe for new machines). Names must not collide, so use `name_prefix` or generated names.
- `prevent_destroy = true`: any plan that would destroy this resource fails. A guard for databases and state buckets. It doesn't help if the block itself is deleted from the code.
- `ignore_changes = [tags, desired_count]`: don't fight changes made outside Terraform to these attributes (for example AWS adding machines automatically under load).
- `replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.version]`: replace this resource when another changes.
- `precondition` and `postcondition` blocks check assumptions (next level).

`terraform_data` (built in, no provider needed) is a handy placeholder resource for triggers, replacing the old `null_resource`.
takeaways: depends_on only for dependencies not expressed by references
create_before_destroy for in-use objects; needs non-colliding names
prevent_destroy guards; ignore_changes stops fights with external changes
pitfalls: Relying on prevent_destroy while deleting the whole resource block: the guard goes with it.

quiz.q: An autoscaler changes desired_count and every apply resets it. Best fix?
quiz.explain: ignore_changes tells Terraform to stop reconciling that attribute after creation.

concepts.name: Writing and using modules
concepts.summary: Group resources into reusable modules with inputs and outputs, and call them from your main configuration.
concepts.why: Modules are how you stop copy-pasting the same VPC or service setup across environments.
concepts.body:
Every Terraform directory is a **module**. The one you run commands in is the **root module**; others are **child modules** called with a `module` block:

`module "network" { source = "./modules/network"  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16" }`

A child module's inputs are its `variable` blocks, and the results it hands back are its `output` blocks. The caller reads outputs as `module.network.vpc_id`. Resources inside are addressed as `module.network.aws_vpc.this`. A module can't see the caller's variables or resources except what is passed in.

Good module design:

- One clear purpose ("a web service with its alarms"), not "everything for team X".
- Small, typed, documented inputs with sensible defaults; checks on important ones (covered later).
- Output the IDs (and AWS ARNs, its full resource names) that callers will need.
- Don't configure providers inside reusable modules; declare `required_providers` and let the root pass configurations (via `providers = { aws = aws.us }` when needed).
- Avoid modules that only wrap a single resource; they add a layer without adding value.

Typical repo layout: `modules/` with reusable modules, and one root directory per environment or component (`envs/prod/network`, `envs/prod/app`) that calls them with environment values.

Run `terraform init` after adding a module; `terraform get` refreshes them.
takeaways: A module = a directory; inputs are variables, results are outputs
Callers use module.<name>.<output>
Don't put provider configuration in reusable modules
pitfalls: Giant do-everything modules with dozens of on/off settings.

quiz.q: How does a root module read a value created inside a child module?
options: Through an output declared in the child, as module.child.<output>
quiz.explain: Only a child module's outputs are visible to its caller.

concepts.name: Module sources, versions and the registry
concepts.summary: Use modules from the Terraform Registry, git repositories and private registries, pinned to versions.
concepts.why: Shared modules save weeks of work, but unpinned ones change underneath you.
concepts.body:
The `source` argument says where a module comes from:

- Local path: `./modules/vpc` (no version; it's your code).
- **Registry**: `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` from the public Terraform Registry, with a `version` constraint such as `~> 6.0`.
- **Git**: `git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//network?ref=v1.4.0`, where `//network` is a subdirectory and `ref` a tag, branch or commit. SSH URLs (`git::ssh://git@github.com/...`) work too, using your SSH keys.
- Private registries (HCP Terraform, Terraform Enterprise, Artifactory, GitLab), and archive files downloaded from a web address or a bucket.

Version pinning matters: registry modules use the `version` argument; git sources pin with `ref`. Tags are convenient but can be moved; a full commit ID can never change.

Evaluate a public module before adopting it: maintainer, activity, how many inputs it has, and whether its design fits your needs. The community `terraform-aws-modules` collection is a common choice for networking and EKS.

`terraform init` downloads modules into `.terraform/modules`; after changing a source or version, run `terraform init -upgrade` (or plain init for a new module).

Publishing your own: a Git repository with version tags (`v1.4.0`) is enough for git sources; the public registry requires the `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>` repository naming.
concepts.code:
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"     # public registry
  version = "~> 6.0"

  name            = "main"
  cidr            = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs             = ["eu-west-1a", "eu-west-1b"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24"]
}

module "service" {
  # git source, subdirectory //ecs-service, pinned to a tag
  source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//ecs-service?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "shop-api"
  vpc_id = module.vpc.vpc_id
}
# terraform init   -> Downloading registry.terraform.io/terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws 6.x.y
takeaways: Registry sources take version; git sources pin with ?ref=
// selects a subdirectory in a repo or archive
Pin modules as carefully as providers
pitfalls: Pointing a git source at a branch like main, so a merge elsewhere changes your next plan.

quiz.q: How do you pin a git-sourced module to release v2.1.0?
quiz.explain: The version argument is for registry modules; git sources use the ref query parameter.

concepts.name: Environments: directories vs workspaces
concepts.summary: Keep dev, staging and production state apart with a folder per environment or with workspaces, and know the trade-offs.
concepts.why: Every team must decide how environments are isolated; the wrong choice risks applying dev changes to prod.
concepts.body:
Each environment needs its own state. Two common approaches:

**Directory per environment** (most common for long-lived environments): `envs/dev`, `envs/staging`, `envs/prod`, each a small root module calling shared modules with its own `backend` key and `.tfvars`. Pros: explicit, environments can differ (prod has a bigger database, dev skips the web firewall), and different credentials or approval rules per directory are easy. Cons: some repetition in the root files.

**Workspaces**: one configuration, several named states. `terraform workspace new staging`, `workspace select prod`, and `terraform.workspace` in expressions. With the S3 backend, non-default workspaces live under the `env:/` prefix. Pros: no duplication, great for short-lived copies (a stack per feature branch). Cons: it's easy to run in the wrong workspace, all environments share the same code version and backend credentials, and differences become conditionals on `terraform.workspace`.

Whatever you choose:

- Also split by **component** (network, data, apps) so each state stays small, plans stay fast, and the blast radius of a mistake is limited.
- Use separate cloud accounts or projects per environment where possible; it's the strongest isolation.
- Make the target environment obvious in automated job names and plan output.

HCP Terraform "workspaces" are a different, richer concept: one per state, with its own variables and permissions.
concepts.code:
# Layout A: directory per environment
# envs/
#   dev/main.tf      module "app" { source = "../../modules/app"  size = "small" }
#   prod/main.tf     module "app" { source = "../../modules/app"  size = "large" }
#   each with backend key ".../dev/terraform.tfstate" or ".../prod/..."

# Layout B: CLI workspaces
terraform workspace new pr-142
terraform workspace list
#   default
# * pr-142
terraform apply -var-file=preview.tfvars   # name resources with terraform.workspace
terraform destroy -auto-approve && terraform workspace select default \
  && terraform workspace delete pr-142
takeaways: Directory per environment: explicit and flexible; workspaces: same code, several states
Split states by component to limit blast radius
Separate accounts/projects per environment is the strongest isolation
pitfalls: Running apply in the prod workspace while thinking you were in dev.

quiz.q: Which approach most easily gives production a different set of resources (e.g. an extra WAF) than dev?
quiz.explain: Separate root modules can differ freely; workspaces share one configuration and need conditionals.

concepts.name: Dynamic blocks and complex collections
concepts.summary: Generate repeated nested blocks with dynamic, and flatten nested data structures for for_each.
concepts.why: Firewall rules, listeners and permission statements often come from data, not fixed code.
concepts.body:
Some arguments are **nested blocks** (`ingress { ... }` inside a security group, `setting { ... }` in an Elastic Beanstalk environment). `count`/`for_each` work only on whole resources, so to generate blocks from a collection you use a **dynamic block**:

`dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules  content { from_port = ingress.value.port ... } }`

The loop variable is named after the block (`ingress.key`, `ingress.value`), or set `iterator = rule`. Use them when the data truly varies; for two fixed blocks, writing them out is clearer.

The other frequent need is **flattening** nested structures for `for_each`. For example, a map of networks each with several subnets: produce one flat list with `flatten`, then key it uniquely:

`{ for s in local.subnet_list : "${s.network}.${s.name}" => s }`

Choose keys that are stable and meaningful, because they become part of resource addresses.

`setproduct` builds combinations (every environment times every region). `try()` and `optional()` attributes with defaults make variable objects pleasant to fill in.

Readability is the real constraint: if a reader needs `terraform console` to understand a local, consider simplifying the input shape instead.
takeaways: dynamic "block" { for_each, content } generates nested blocks
flatten nested data, then build a map with stable unique keys
Prefer explicit blocks when the set is small and fixed
pitfalls: Using list positions as keys after flattening, which brings back count's index-shift problem.

quiz.q: Inside dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.rules ... }, how do you refer to the current rule?
quiz.explain: The iterator in a dynamic block is named after the block unless you set iterator.

concepts.name: Refactoring: moved, import and removed
concepts.summary: Rename and restructure without recreating resources, bring existing infrastructure under management, and let go of resources safely.
concepts.why: Code changes shape over time; without these tools every rename or adoption risks destroying live resources.
concepts.body:
Resource addresses are identities. Change one (rename, move into a module, switch from count to for_each) and Terraform sees a destroy plus a create, unless you tell it otherwise.

**moved blocks** record a rename in code:

`moved { from = aws_s3_bucket.logs  to = module.logs.aws_s3_bucket.this }`

The next plan shows "has moved to" instead of destroy/create. Keep moved blocks for a while, as other environments may not have applied them yet. They are reviewable, unlike the older `terraform state mv` command.

**import blocks** adopt existing objects (made in the console or by another tool):

`import { to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy  id = "acme-legacy-bucket" }`

Plan shows what will be imported and any differences from your configuration. `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf` even writes a starting configuration for you to clean up. `for_each` in import blocks adopts many at once. The ID format depends on the resource type; see each resource's Import section in the provider docs.

**removed blocks** take a resource out of state without destroying it, when another configuration should own it, or it should just be left alone:

`removed { from = aws_instance.old  lifecycle { destroy = false } }`

All three are applied as part of a normal plan/apply, so they get the same review as any other change.
takeaways: moved: rename without recreate
import (+ -generate-config-out): adopt existing objects
removed with destroy = false: stop managing without deleting
pitfalls: Renaming a resource without a moved block and approving a plan that destroys it.

quiz.q: You switch a resource from count to for_each. How do you avoid recreating the existing instance aws_iam_user.u[0] (user ana)?
options: A moved block from aws_iam_user.u[0] to aws_iam_user.u["ana"]
An import block for each user
quiz.explain: moved maps the old address to the new one so state is rewritten instead of recreating.

concepts.name: Validation, pre/postconditions and checks
concepts.summary: Reject bad inputs with variable validation, assert assumptions with pre/postconditions, and monitor with check blocks.
concepts.why: Failing early with a clear message beats a half-applied plan or a silently wrong deployment.
concepts.body:
Terraform has several assertion mechanisms, each for a different moment:

- **Variable validation**: inside a `variable`, one or more `validation { condition = ... error_message = "..." }` blocks. Evaluated at plan time. Since 1.9 conditions may also refer to other variables and resources, not only the variable itself.
- **precondition** (in a resource's, data source's or output's `lifecycle`): checked before that resource is planned or applied. Good for assumptions about inputs or looked-up data ("the machine image must be built for 64-bit Intel or AMD chips").
- **postcondition**: checked after the resource is created or read, with `self` referring to it ("the machine must have received a public address").
- **check blocks**: top-level `check "name" { assert {...} }`, optionally with a scoped data source, run on every plan and apply. A failure is a **warning**, not an error, so checks suit continuous health assertions like "the website returns 200".

Write error messages for the person who will hit them: say what's wrong and what to do.

Use `can()` in conditions to turn errors into booleans: `can(regex("^[a-z0-9-]+$", var.name))`. Keep conditions simple; complex logic hides mistakes.

These checks complement, and don't replace, `terraform test` and policy tools (OPA/conftest, Sentinel) that judge the plan as a whole.
takeaways: validation for inputs; pre/postconditions for assumptions about resources
check blocks warn on every run without stopping it
can() turns failing expressions into false
pitfalls: Vague error messages like 'invalid input' that don't tell users how to fix it.

quiz.q: Which mechanism reports a failure as a warning rather than stopping the apply?
quiz.explain: check block assertions produce warnings so they can monitor without blocking changes.

concepts.name: Testing modules with terraform test
concepts.summary: Write .tftest.hcl files with run blocks and assertions, using plan-only runs and mocked providers.
concepts.why: Shared modules are code that many teams depend on; they need automated tests too.
concepts.body:
`terraform test` runs test files (`*.tftest.hcl`, in the module root or `tests/`). Each file contains **run** blocks executed in order:

- `command = plan` checks the plan only: fast and needs no real infrastructure for many assertions.
- `command = apply` (the default) actually creates the resources, runs assertions, and **destroys everything** at the end of the file.
- `variables { ... }` at file or run level set inputs.
- `assert { condition = ... error_message = ... }` blocks check outputs and resource attributes, e.g. `aws_s3_bucket.this.bucket == "acme-logs"`.
- `expect_failures = [var.env]` asserts that validation rejects bad input: test your error paths.
- `module { source = "./tests/setup" }` in a run block uses a helper module, for example to create things the test needs first or to load test data.

**Mocking** (`mock_provider "aws" {}` in a test file) replaces a provider with one that returns fake values, so even apply-style tests run in seconds without credentials. Combine: unit-style tests with mocks on every commit, tests that really apply, nightly, in a separate throwaway account.

Run with `terraform test`, or `terraform test -filter=tests/naming.tftest.hcl` for one file. Results print pass/fail per run block.

Terratest (Go) remains an option for complex end-to-end checks, such as making HTTP requests to what you deployed.
takeaways: run blocks with command = plan or apply, plus assert blocks
expect_failures tests validation errors
mock_provider makes tests fast and credential-free
pitfalls: Running apply-mode tests in a production account; use a sandbox, since tests create real resources.

quiz.q: What happens to resources created by apply-mode run blocks when the test file finishes?
options: They are moved to the root state
They are imported into a workspace
quiz.explain: terraform test cleans up everything it created at the end of each file.

concepts.name: Terraform in CI/CD
concepts.summary: Run plans on pull requests, apply the reviewed plan on merge, and sign in with short-lived credentials.
concepts.why: Applying from laptops doesn't scale; automation makes every change reviewed, logged and repeatable.
concepts.body:
A typical pull-request workflow:

1. On every pull request: `terraform fmt -check`, `terraform init`, `terraform validate`, linters (TFLint), security scanners (Trivy, Checkov), then `terraform plan -out=tfplan`, posting a plan summary to the pull request.
2. Reviewers read the plan, not only the code.
3. On merge (or approval): `terraform apply tfplan` with the reviewed plan, or a fresh plan plus a manual approval step.

Practical details:

- Set `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1` (shorter output) and `-input=false`, so nothing waits for typed input.
- Credentials: let the CI system sign in with **OIDC** (OpenID Connect: GitHub Actions or GitLab vouches for the job, and the cloud swaps that for short-lived credentials) instead of long-lived access keys. Give plan jobs a read-only role and apply jobs the write role.
- Allow only one apply per state at a time (in GitHub Actions, a concurrency group), on top of state locking.

- Cache downloaded providers (`TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR`) to speed up init.
- Policy checks (OPA/conftest on `terraform show -json tfplan`, Sentinel in HCP Terraform) can block forbidden changes such as public buckets.
- Run a scheduled `plan -detailed-exitcode` to spot drift, changes made outside Terraform: exit code 2 means changes are pending.

Tools like HCP Terraform, Atlantis, Spacelift and env0 implement this workflow for you, including locking and pull request comments.
concepts.code:
# .github/workflows/terraform.yml (core steps)
name: terraform
on: [pull_request]
permissions: {id-token: write, contents: read, pull-requests: write}
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env: {TF_IN_AUTOMATION: "1"}
    defaults: {run: {working-directory: envs/prod}}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with: {role-to-assume: "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/tf-plan", aws-region: eu-west-1}
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt   # post as a PR comment
takeaways: Plan on PRs, review the plan, apply the saved plan on merge
OIDC short-lived credentials; read-only for plan, write for apply
-detailed-exitcode on a schedule detects drift
pitfalls: Storing long-lived admin cloud keys as CI secrets for Terraform.

quiz.q: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode exits with code 2. What does that mean?
options: The plan succeeded and there are changes to apply
quiz.explain: 0 means no changes, 1 an error, 2 success with a non-empty diff.

concepts.name: State internals, refresh and drift
concepts.summary: Understand the state file's serial and lineage, refresh-only plans, drift handling and safe state surgery.
concepts.why: When something goes wrong with state, you need to know exactly what Terraform stores and how it reconciles.
concepts.body:
The state file is JSON with a `version` (format), `terraform_version`, a **serial** (incremented on every write) and a **lineage** (a random ID fixed when the state was created). Backends refuse to overwrite a state with a different lineage or an older serial, which protects against pushing an old or unrelated copy. Each resource stores its attributes, the version of its provider's data format, its dependencies and which values are sensitive.

**Drift** is a difference between state and reality caused by changes outside Terraform. A normal plan refreshes first and reports "Objects have changed outside of Terraform" before proposing to put things back according to your configuration.

- `terraform plan -refresh-only` / `apply -refresh-only` accepts reality into state without changing infrastructure; use it to acknowledge legitimate external changes, then update the code to match.
- `-refresh=false` skips reading real objects (faster, riskier), useful in huge states or outages.

State surgery commands, all of which take the lock and write a backup:

- `terraform state rm` forgets a resource (prefer a `removed` block).
- `terraform state mv` renames (prefer `moved`).
- `terraform state pull > backup.tfstate` / `state push` for disaster recovery; push checks lineage and serial unless forced.

Recovering from a corrupted remote state usually means restoring an earlier object version from the bucket's versioning. That's why versioning is non-negotiable.
concepts.code:
terraform state pull | jq '{version, serial, lineage, terraform_version,
  resources: [.resources[] | "\(.type).\(.name)"]}'
# { "version": 4, "serial": 42, "lineage": "8f0c2c1e-...",
#   "terraform_version": "1.14.0", "resources": ["aws_vpc.main", ...] }

terraform plan
# Note: Objects have changed outside of Terraform
#   ~ tags = { + "owner" = "ana" }    (added in the console)

terraform apply -refresh-only      # accept the drift into state
terraform state pull > backup-$(date +%F).tfstate
takeaways: serial increments per write; lineage identifies one state's history
-refresh-only accepts outside changes without touching infrastructure
Back up with state pull; recover via bucket versioning
pitfalls: Using state push -force with an old copy, overwriting newer state and orphaning resources.

quiz.q: Someone changed a tag in the console and the team agrees it should stay. What is the cleanest sequence?
options: Update the configuration to include the tag, then plan shows no changes
Run state rm on the resource
quiz.explain: Making the code match reality removes the drift; apply -refresh-only can update state meanwhile.

concepts.name: The dependency graph and execution
concepts.summary: How Terraform builds a resource graph, walks it in parallel, handles unknown values and orders replacements.
concepts.why: Explains slow plans, odd ordering, "known after apply" cascades and cycle errors.
concepts.body:
Terraform builds a **directed acyclic graph** from your configuration, a map of items joined by one-way arrows with no loops: nodes for resources, data sources, providers, variables, locals, outputs and modules; edges from references and `depends_on`. `terraform graph` prints it in Graphviz's DOT text format.

Execution walks the graph concurrently: any node whose dependencies are done can run, up to `-parallelism=10` operations at a time by default. Lower it when an API rate-limits you; raise it for large flat states.

Order details:

- Destroys run in the reverse of creation order.
- With `create_before_destroy`, the replacement is created before the old object (and everything depending on it) is destroyed; the setting propagates to dependencies to keep the graph acyclic.
- A **cycle** error means two objects depend on each other through references; break it by splitting a resource (e.g. separate security group rule resources instead of inline rules).

**Unknown values**: attributes computed by the provider during apply are unknown at plan time. They propagate: anything derived from them becomes `(known after apply)`, which can force replacements to look broader than they are, and make `count`/`for_each` impossible to evaluate ("value depends on resource attributes that cannot be determined until apply"). Fix by keying on known inputs, or splitting into two applies with `-target` as a last resort.

Plan time grows with the number of resources and the API calls refresh makes; splitting large states is the main cure.
concepts.code:
terraform graph -type=plan | dot -Tsvg > graph.svg   # needs graphviz

terraform apply -parallelism=4        # gentler on rate-limited APIs

# Classic unknown-value error:
# Error: Invalid for_each argument
#   The "for_each" map includes keys derived from resource attributes
#   that cannot be determined until apply...
# Fix: key on input values (names), not on IDs created in the same run.

# Cycle example message:
# Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.a, aws_security_group.b
# Fix: move the cross-references into separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources.
takeaways: References and depends_on form a DAG walked in parallel (default 10)
Unknown values propagate and can block count/for_each
Cycles are fixed by splitting resources
pitfalls: Keying for_each on IDs of resources created in the same apply.

quiz.q: Why does for_each = { for i in aws_instance.web : i.id => i } fail on a fresh apply?
options: The instance IDs aren't known until apply, so the keys can't be planned
quiz.explain: for_each keys must be known at plan time; new IDs are only known after apply.

concepts.name: How providers work
concepts.summary: Providers are separate programs Terraform talks to over gRPC; understand schemas, the lock file's hashes, mirrors and dev overrides.
concepts.why: Air-gapped installs, checksum errors, provider upgrades and custom providers all depend on this model.
concepts.body:
Terraform core knows nothing about clouds. Each **provider** is a separate program that Terraform starts and talks to over **gRPC**, a standard way for one program to call another (plugin protocol version 5 or 6). Core asks it for its **schema** (resource types, attributes, which are computed or force replacement), then calls operations such as `PlanResourceChange`, `ApplyResourceChange`, `ReadResource` and `ImportResourceState`. The provider translates them into API calls.

Consequences you'll notice:

- "forces replacement" decisions come from the provider's schema and plan logic, not from Terraform core.
- Provider upgrades can change defaults or schemas; a resource's **schema version** with state upgraders migrates stored attributes. Read changelogs for major versions.
- Bugs that look like Terraform bugs are usually provider bugs; check the provider's issue tracker.

**Installation**: `init` resolves versions from the registry, downloads the zip for your OS/architecture, and verifies its signature. `.terraform.lock.hcl` stores `h1:` and `zh:` checksums; on another platform the hash may be missing, so run `terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64` to record all you need.

For restricted networks use `terraform providers mirror` to a directory and configure `provider_installation` in the CLI config (`~/.terraformrc`) with `filesystem_mirror` or `network_mirror`. For provider development, `dev_overrides` points at a local build.

New providers are written in Go with the **Terraform Plugin Framework**.
takeaways: Providers are plugin processes talking gRPC to core
Replacement and defaults come from provider schemas
Lock file hashes per platform; mirrors for restricted networks
pitfalls: Generating the lock file on macOS only, so Linux CI fails checksum verification.

quiz.q: CI on Linux fails with a provider checksum mismatch, while it works on your Mac. Likely fix?
options: Delete the lock file in CI
Run terraform providers lock with both platforms and commit the result
quiz.explain: The lock file only had hashes for your platform; record hashes for all platforms you use.

concepts.name: Secrets, sensitive and ephemeral values
concepts.summary: Know what ends up in state and plans, and keep secrets out with ephemeral resources, ephemeral variables and write-only arguments.
concepts.why: State has historically held every secret in plain text; modern Terraform can avoid that.
concepts.body:
`sensitive = true` on variables and outputs, and values a provider marks as sensitive, only **hide them on screen**: plans and logs show `(sensitive value)`, but the value is still written to state and to saved plan files. So treat state and plan files as secrets: encrypted storage, tight access, and never publish plan files as downloads of a public CI run.

Newer features keep values out of artifacts entirely:

- **Ephemeral variables and outputs** (`ephemeral = true`, 1.10+): available during the run, never saved in state or plan. They can only flow into places that accept ephemeral values.
- **Ephemeral resources** (`ephemeral "aws_secretsmanager_secret_version" "db" {...}`): fetch a secret or a temporary credential for the duration of the run, e.g. to configure a provider, without saving it.
- **Write-only arguments** (1.11+): resource arguments like `password_wo` (with a companion `password_wo_version` to signal changes) that are sent to the API but never stored. Support depends on the provider and resource.

Other options: have the service generate and own the secret (RDS `manage_master_user_password = true` stores it in Secrets Manager), or pass references (an ARN) rather than values.

Avoid `random_password` resources whose result lands in state, unless state is protected accordingly. OpenTofu additionally offers client-side state encryption.
takeaways: sensitive hides output but values still land in state and plans
ephemeral variables/resources are never persisted
Write-only arguments send secrets without storing them; bump the version to change
pitfalls: Believing sensitive = true keeps a password out of the state file.

quiz.q: Which feature keeps a database password out of the state file entirely?
options: A write-only argument fed from an ephemeral variable
quiz.explain: sensitive only redacts display; ephemeral values into write-only arguments are never persisted.
